Persona-Conditioned Reward Model Rankings

All 49 personas scored, across 5 prompt templates (245 persona×template combinations, each against both baselines)

Full vocabulary scored per prompt (every token, exhaustively) — R-Lla-3B: 128,249 tokens · R-Lla-3B: 128,250 tokens

About this dashboard

Each panel compares a reward model's token-level scoring of a prompt with an “I am <persona>” prefix against a baseline — i.e. does an identity prefix change what the model rewards? The Baseline dropdown above switches which comparison point is used everywhere: the plain, no-persona prompt, or the same prompt with the control persona (“a person”) substituted in. The neutral baseline answers "does this persona change anything at all"; the control baseline isolates a persona's specific identity content from the effect of any "I am X" prefix (which alone can shift the ranking, independent of who "X" is). Agreement with the baseline (bar chart, scatter below) measures that shift directly: Kendall’s τ for whole-distribution agreement, RBO for top-of-ranking agreement (RBO can diverge from τ when the broad ranking is stable but the top answer specifically changes). Base LM vs. reward model asks whether that shift is inherited from the underlying language model or introduced by reward-model fine-tuning — points off the diagonal implicate the fine-tuning step (hover a token in the detail tables below for the same comparison at the individual-token level). Prompt-framing comparison and persona consistency across framings ask a different question, independent of baseline: does simply rewording “the same” question move the ranking — and is that framing-sensitivity itself persona-dependent, or uniform across personas?

Reference: the neutral prompt, with no persona at all

What the model prefers with no “I am X” prefix, for whichever prompt framing is selected above — shown below with the exact prompt text used. Every persona comparison above is measured against this.

Agreement with the neutral baseline, by persona

Kendall’s τ across the full token vocabulary. Bars near zero mean the persona-conditioned ranking has little in common with the plain, no-persona prompt. Solid bars are the reward model; lighter dashed bars (when present) are the base LM's own persona-shift τ for comparison. Click a bar for token-level detail.

Token-level detail — reward model

Click a persona above to see its highest/lowest scoring tokens and the tokens whose rank shifted most vs. the neutral baseline.

Hover a token row (when base-LM data is available) to see whether it shows a similar movement in the base LM’s own persona-conditioned logits — helps tell effects inherited from pretraining apart from ones introduced by reward-model fine-tuning.

Token-level detail — base LM

Same comparison as above, but using the base LM's own persona-conditioned logits and its own baseline instead of the reward model's scores.

Whole-distribution vs. top-of-ranking agreement

τ captures agreement across the whole vocabulary; RBO (p=0.95) weights the very top of the ranking — i.e. what the model would actually prefer. Personas low on RBO but not-as-low on τ are reshaping the top answer specifically, not the whole distribution. Click a dot for token-level detail.

Base LM vs. reward model persona sensitivity

x = the base LM's own persona-shift metric (its persona-conditioned logits vs. its own neutral baseline); y = the reward model's persona-shift metric for the same persona/template. Points near the diagonal mean the RM mostly inherits the base LM's persona sensitivity; points off the diagonal mean reward-model finetuning changed it.

No base-LM logit data yet for this model — run generate_base_model_logprobs.py --config llama_base_models.yaml and generate_persona_base_model_logprobs.py, then rerun analyze_personas.py.

Prompt-framing comparison

How similar are different phrasings of “the same” question, for the same persona? Between every pair of templates that share an underlying question (e.g. the four “greatest thing ever” framings), shown side by side as mean Kendall’s τ (whole-distribution agreement, across all scored personas) and mean RBO p=0.95 (top-of-ranking agreement, which can diverge from τ). One pair of heatmaps per question group, plus the same pair for a single persona directly below. Click a cell for token-level detail.

Same comparison as the heatmap(s) above, but for one persona directly (not averaged across all personas) — shows whether framing-sensitivity is uniform or persona-specific.

Persona consistency across prompt framings

Mean Kendall’s τ between every pair of templates in a question group, per persona — low bars mean this persona's reward-model ranking shifts a lot depending on how the question is phrased, even though the persona itself didn't change.

Each persona comparison is measured against the baseline selected above (see the reference panel for the exact text) — either the matching no-persona prompt, or the same prompt with the control persona substituted in, which isolates the effect of a specific identity from the effect of any “I am X” prefix at all. The original one-word “greatest”/“best”/“worst” neutral baselines are from Christian et al. (2025); the matched in-sentence framings (plain, “I think”, “you think”, “people think”) and the control-persona baseline were generated for this persona extension. Persona categories from Wang et al. (2025).
